items.title: Adaptations to the problems of Photorespiration

source_refs.note: Adaptations to the problems of Photorespiration, printed pages 162-164 (PDF 165-167); a main subheading of Photorespiration, its own page as in Computer Science (owner 2026-11-04).

blocks.text: Plants of warmer climates evolved the following two ways to deal with the problem of photorespiration.
C-4 plants carry out C-4 as well as C-3 photosynthesis.

Some plants including grasses (corn, sugarcane and sorghum) and about two dozen other plant groups run a special pathway called C-4 photosynthesis in addition to the normal Calvin cycle. In their leaves, the mesophyll cells have less air spaces. The enzymes of Calvin cycle are more deposited in specialized cells called bundle-sheath cells, which are impermeable to CO₂.

In C-4 photosynthesis, the energy cost for making a glucose molecule is almost double. However, in hot climates, in which photorespiration would otherwise remove more than half of the carbon fixed, it is best compromise available.

During C-4 photosynthesis (Fig 5.22) in mesophyll cells, CO₂, is attached with a 3-carbon molecule called phosphoenol pyruvic acid. It results in the formation of a four-carbon molecule oxaloacetic acid. Due to this first 4-C product, this process is called C-4 photosynthesis and the plants are called C-4 plants. Oxaloacetic acid is then converted to malic acid, by using NADH. Malic acid is transported to an adjacent bundle-sheath cell. Here, malic acid is broken down to pyruvic acid and CO₂. These cells can hold CO₂ in them. So, concentration of CO₂ increases in these cells and they run Calvin cycle instead of photorespiration. Pyruvic acid produced in bundle sheath cells returns to mesophyll cell and is converted again to phosphoenol pyruvic acid b using an ATP.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the mesophyll cells of C-4 plants such as maize and sugarcane, oxaloacetic acid is reduced to malic acid by NADPH (made in the light reactions), not NADH: oxaloacetic acid is then converted to malic acid, using NADPH.

blocks.alt: Left, C-3 Photosynthesis: in a mesophyll cell CO2 enters the Calvin cycle with RuBP and sugar leaves. Right, C-4 Photosynthesis: in the mesophyll cell CO2 joins phosphoenol pyruvic acid (3-C) to form oxaloacetic acid (4-C), which becomes malic acid (4-C); malic acid passes into the bundle sheath cell and splits into CO2, which enters the Calvin cycle with RuBP to make sugar, and pyruvic acid (3-C), which returns to the mesophyll cell and becomes phosphoenol pyruvic acid again.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.22: C-3 photosynthesis and C-4 photosynthesis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.22).

blocks.text: In hot climates, many succulent plants such as Cacti, pineapples and some other plant groups perform Crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM (after the plant family Crassulaceae in which it was first discovered). In these plants, the stomata open during the night and close during the day. Closing stomata during the day prevents water loss and removal of CO₂. So, rate of photorespiration is reduced due to high concentration of carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide necessary for producing sugar is provided from organic molecules made the night before. Like C-4 plants, these plants use both C-4 and C-3 pathways.
